# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Critical Reading: Varga & Holm Comment on the Halden Pilot

**Bottom line:** Sections 1–5 are a valuable re-analysis. They use the microdata to confirm, with numbers, most of the weaknesses suspected in the Halden paper, and they uncover a serious misstatement about attrition. Sections 6–8 then go well beyond the evidence. The claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is not supported by the authors' own corrected estimate. It is contradicted by their own data note, and it ignores the randomised Varden result that cuts against it.

## 1. Arithmetic check

**Correct:**
- **Table 2:** 95.1 / 0.8 gives +18.9%; 98.4 / 0.859 gives +14.6%; 95.4 / 0.861 gives +10.8%.
- **Hours ratios:** 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 (a 14.1% fall) and 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 (a 13.9% fall).
- **Real revenue:** 1.014 / 1.041 gives −2.6%.
- **Table 1:** 98.9 − 95.1 = 3.8 points.

**Doesn't reconcile: the hours breakdown in §3.**
- Actual pilot hours were 34.6, which is 2.6 hours above the 32 scheduled.
- But the two sources given add up to 4.4 hours: 4 days × 0.7 extra hours = 2.8, plus 1.6 hours on the day off.
- Measured from the actual baseline day of 8.06 hours, the components imply about 36.6 hours a week, not 34.6.

Either the components are defined differently from what the text says (for example, day-off work averaged only over those who worked it), or there is an error. The authors should reconcile this, since the hours correction is central to their argument.

## 2. What's strong

**Attrition (§1).** This is the most important new finding.
- Halden said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons."
- The microdata show that seven of the nine left after the reduced schedule had started.
- Six of the nine cited workload or inability to maintain output.

This is a material misstatement in the original paper, not a matter of interpretation. Halden's results describe the organisations that survived the change.

**Output measure (§2).**
- Managers' ratings exceeded their own organisations' records in 19 of 23 cases.
- That is a systematic bias, not noise.
- The authors frame it fairly, as optimism rather than bad faith.

**Hours (§3).** Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%. This closely matches Varden's timesheet result of a 13–17% fall, so two independent sources agree.

**Revenue and sectors (§4–5).**
- Both points are sound: the revenue rise is nominal, and any output index above 80 shows a per-hour "gain."
- Retail's record-based fall of 11.2% matches Varden's counter-office fall of 11.4%.
- However, the retail figure rests on only three organisations.

**Recommendations (§8).** Record-based output, actual hours, a comparison group, long follow-up and intention-to-treat analysis are all appropriate.

## 3. Where it overreaches

### a. Attrition is said to be corrected, but it isn't

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems, which includes attrition, brings the gain down to 10.8%. But Table 2 corrects only output and hours. The withdrawn organisations appear in no estimate.

The direction of the attrition bias is credible: it would push the gain down. Its size is unmeasured. That is a reason for more uncertainty, not a demonstrated reduction.

### b. The revenue problem doesn't affect the per-hour figure

The abstract says "four problems... account for most of the reported gain," but the revenue figure plays no part in computing the per-hour gain. Revenue is a fair criticism of how Halden presented its results, but it doesn't belong in that sentence.

### c. The conclusion contradicts the data note

- The data note says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole."
- The conclusion then generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.
- The 17 organisations with both records and time tracking are a non-random subset of a non-random set of survivors.
- No confidence interval is given for 10.8% or for any other estimate. With 17 clusters, the interval will be wide.

### d. The novelty argument is untested and rests on weak extrapolation

- **No output data on timing:** The residual gain is attributed to novelty on the basis of self-reported energy, not output. Energy and output per hour are different measures.
- **The direct test was available but not run:** Halden collected the output index monthly. If novelty drove the gain, output per hour should decline from month 3 to month 6 in the microdata. The authors had the data and don't report this trajectory.
- **Two-point extrapolation:** A straight line through 0.61 at month 3 and 0.29 at month 6 reaches zero around month 9, not month 10. More importantly, two points can't distinguish decay toward zero from levelling off at a higher level.
- **Misplaced burden of proof:** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is a reasonable standard for claiming that an effect lasts. But failing to prove persistence is not the same as proving the effect is an artifact.

### e. The Varden evidence is used selectively

- The Comment calls Varden's counter-office finding "the most reliable finding in the literature."
- It ignores Varden's case-processing result: +12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4).
- That result is randomised, uses administrative output and timesheet hours, and runs nine months against a control group. A control group addresses general trends, though not the effect of staff knowing they're in a trial.
- This is the strongest evidence that some per-hour gain is real in work where output doesn't depend on staff presence. It runs directly against "entirely an artifact."
- Varden's +12.5% is also very close to the Comment's own corrected +10.8%. Two different methods landing in the same place is better read as convergence than as artifact.
- The Comment also omits that Varden found sick days fell 29% relative to control, a randomised finding. "The best-supported finding is the negative one" overlooks it.

### f. Varden's meetings analysis is mischaracterised

- **Strength of claim:** Varden didn't present meetings as an established mechanism. It said they "may account for part" of the gain, stated that seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test. The Comment's statistical caution is fair, but Varden had already made the same point.
- **Selection:** "Selected for analysis after the results were known" is inaccurate. The data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results. The correlation used all seven treated case-processing offices, not a hand-picked subgroup.
- **Fair question it doesn't ask:** Why weren't meeting data reported for the counter offices?
- **What follows:** The right conclusion is "unconfirmed, awaiting the registered test," not "should not be cited."

### g. Smaller points

- **Billable hours as output:** Some of the records used to measure output are billable hours. For professional services, billable hours partly measure time rather than output, so this choice may push the record-based index down mechanically.
- **Consumer prices as deflator:** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue; producer or sector prices would be better. The direction of the correction is still right.

## 4. Where the three documents leave things

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Was Halden's 23.4% accurate? | No. Biased manager ratings, scheduled rather than actual hours, and survivor-only results all inflated it. |
| Is there a per-hour gain in work not tied to presence? | Probably about 10–13%, from Varden's randomised trial and the Comment's corrected subset. Persistence is unproven. |
| Is that gain "free" to employers? | Unclear. Varden found overtime, and no study reports cost. |
| Coverage-bound work? | Output per employee and service fall by about 11%. |
| Sick days? | They fall, and Varden confirms this with a randomised design. |
| Mechanism (fatigue, meetings, novelty)? | Unresolved. Varden's registered test and its 24-month follow-up are the key pending evidence. |

The Comment strengthens the case against Halden's headline but not the case for "entirely an artifact." Its own corrected figure and the Varden trial both point to a smaller per-hour gain in work not tied to presence, with persistence still unproven.
